::: {.kw-overview}
This issue starts with the drugs recipients take for reasons other than immunosuppression. A small single-centre open-label trial gives dapagliflozin a fragile 54-week glomerular filtration rate signal in post-transplant diabetes that weakens once more covariates are added, and a propensity-matched American cohort of more than 23,000 recipients ties continued proton pump inhibitor use to roughly twice the hazard of graft failure, an association plausible enough to justify a deprescribing review even though the design cannot show cause. Infection prevention gets two practical answers. In a Thai randomised trial the licensed high-dose influenza vaccine produced seroconversion in 95% of recipients against 69% with two standard doses given at one visit, and a Swiss–Danish cohort of 2,057 kidney recipients, part of a wider transplant cohort, finds three months of antiviral prophylaxis as good as six for donor-positive, recipient-negative non-lung recipients. On rejection risk, a Utah cohort of 657 recipients links class II eplet mismatch load to early allograft injury while conceding that it discriminates no better than antigen-level mismatch. Donor utilisation closes the issue. A meta-analysis puts the cost of each 10-point rise in kidney donor profile index at a 19% higher hazard of death-censored graft failure, a South Carolina programme used overnight machine perfusion and booked morning theatre to turn deceased-donor transplantation into semi-elective surgery, and an analysis of American procurement organisations suggests that the 2025 clampdown on out-of-sequence allocation cost kidney transplants by reducing recoveries, not by making recovered kidneys harder to place.
:::

### 1. [Dapagliflozin and 54-week kidney function in kidney transplant recipients with post-transplant diabetes mellitus: a randomized controlled trial](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2026.113605)
[Li J, Fu Z, Xu R, Zhuang Y, Chen P, Chen J. *Diabetes Res Clin Pract*, 2026. PMID: 42874781.]{.kw-ref}

Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are going into transplant recipients well ahead of trial evidence, so any randomised data in this population are welcome, even from a small study. This single-centre, open-label trial assigned 68 recipients with post-transplant diabetes 1:1 to dapagliflozin 10 mg daily on top of standard care or to standard care alone, and followed kidney function to week 54. Only 27 participants per arm had observed data at that point, so the investigators also ran an intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation that included everyone randomised. Adjusted for baseline, estimated glomerular filtration rate was 6.81 mL/min/1.73 m² higher with dapagliflozin in the complete-case analysis (95% confidence interval 1.68 to 11.94; p = 0.010) and 6.05 mL/min/1.73 m² higher after imputation (0.99 to 11.11; p = 0.020). With further multivariable adjustment the difference shrank and its confidence interval included zero. HbA1c and tacrolimus troughs did not differ between arms, serum magnesium fell less on dapagliflozin, and adverse events occurred at similar frequencies, although the trial was not powered to detect uncommon harms. The authors call the kidney finding exploratory and say the trial does not show a definite, clinically meaningful benefit, which is the correct reading of a result that moves with the choice of covariates and missing-data assumptions. For UK units already giving SGLT2 inhibitors to transplant recipients with diabetes, the trial offers some reassurance on tacrolimus levels and short-term tolerability, but it does not establish graft protection. That needs a larger, blinded trial.

### 2. [Proton pump inhibitor use after kidney transplantation and graft outcomes: A matched national cohort study](https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000051046)
[Aly AE, Sadda VR, Venard E, Ekhtiar T, Powers C, Darby SL, Zheng P, Ayazi S. *Medicine (Baltimore)*, 2026. PMID: 42854000.]{.kw-ref}

Many recipients stay on a proton pump inhibitor long after transplant, often with no clearly documented reason for it. This study used the TriNetX federated electronic record network to identify 23,306 adult kidney recipients transplanted in the United States between 2000 and 2021, entered them into the cohort four to six weeks after surgery, and compared those still taking a proton pump inhibitor beyond the first month (15,601, or 66.9%) with those taking none. After 1:1 propensity matching on demographics, comorbidity, one-month graft function and immunosuppression, 7,553 pairs remained. Graft failure in the first year was 16.8% against 9.4% (hazard ratio 1.79, 95% confidence interval 1.59 to 2.01), and between years one and five 12.8% against 4.7% (hazard ratio 2.63, 2.27 to 3.05). Five-year graft survival was 72.6% against 85.8%. The full text adds several dose-response-like findings. Taking a proton pump inhibitor before transplant did not matter by itself, but continuing it afterwards did (hazard ratio 2.72 for late failure compared with stopping). Use beyond one year carried more late risk than shorter courses (hazard ratio 2.35). Users also did worse than recipients on H2-receptor antagonists (hazard ratio 1.59 for late failure). The limits are serious, and the authors acknowledge them: outcomes depend on diagnostic and procedure codes, and donor type, donor characteristics, rejection episodes and BK virus infection could not be included in the matching because the dataset does not hold them reliably, which leaves ample room for confounding by indication. Even so, the size and consistency of the signal make a UK pharmacy-led review of every long-term proton pump inhibitor in clinic a low-cost step, with an H2-receptor antagonist worth considering where acid suppression is genuinely needed.

### 3. [Immunogenicity and safety of high-dose versus double-dose quadrivalent inactivated influenza vaccine in adult kidney transplant recipients: a randomized controlled trial (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lansea.2026.100873)
[Arayanumas T, Boonnak K, Kantachuvesiri S, Boongird S, Kiertiburanakul S, Bruminhent J. *Lancet Reg Health Southeast Asia*, 2026. PMID: 42831180.]{.kw-ref}

Where high-dose influenza vaccine is scarce or expensive, giving two standard doses at the same visit is an obvious workaround. This open-label trial at a single Bangkok centre tested whether that workaround is good enough. During the 2023 Southern Hemisphere season, 88 stable adult kidney recipients at least three months after transplant were randomised to the 60 μg-per-strain high-dose quadrivalent vaccine or to two standard doses given in opposite arms (30 μg per strain in total), and 84 (42 per arm) had paired haemagglutination-inhibition titres at four weeks. Mean age was 46 years, 60.7% had deceased-donor kidneys and all were on prednisolone. Seroconversion to at least one strain was 95.2% with high dose against 69.0% with double dose (absolute difference 26 percentage points, 95% confidence interval 12 to 40; p = 0.002). Strain-level seroconversion favoured high dose throughout but was individually significant only for B/Yamagata (61.9% against 40.5%), and post-vaccination geometric mean titres and seroprotection did not differ significantly. On multivariable analysis, high dose (odds ratio 17.59) and vaccination more than a year after transplant (odds ratio 34.76) both independently predicted seroconversion, with very wide intervals. The full text adds an important interaction: the high-dose advantage appeared only beyond the first post-transplant year and was absent within it. Injection-site pain and myalgia were less frequent with high dose, all reactions were grade 1, and no rejection occurred. The endpoint is serological, not clinical influenza, and the sample is small. Still, for UK centres it supports using high-dose vaccine for established recipients and suggests that early recipients need another strategy, because a larger dose does not appear to overcome early post-transplant immunosuppression.

### 4. [Prophylaxis Durations and Risks of Cytomegalovirus Infection and Disease in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients: An International, Multicenter Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.1111/tid.70321)
[Dahl AL, Manuel O, Koller M, Reekie J, Tusch E, Moestrup K, Perch M, Rossing K, Schultz N, Sorensen SS, Schønning K, Lundgren J, Mueller NJ, Helleberg M. *Transpl Infect Dis*, 2026. PMID: 42855943.]{.kw-ref}

How long to give antiviral prophylaxis after transplantation remains unsettled, and this cohort uses variation in practice between centres to look at that question. Investigators followed every donor-positive/recipient-negative or recipient-positive transplant recipient in Zürich, Lausanne and Copenhagen between 2008 and 2022 for 12 months, giving 3,203 non-lung recipients (2,057 of them kidney, 815 liver, 331 heart) and 620 lung recipients. They related prophylaxis duration, which ranged from none to 12 months or more, to cytomegalovirus infection and disease using multivariable Poisson regression. In donor-positive/recipient-negative non-lung recipients, relying on pre-emptive monitoring with no prophylaxis carried a higher risk than three months of prophylaxis, both for infection (adjusted incidence rate ratio 2.46, 95% confidence interval 1.69 to 3.57) and for disease (2.82, 1.18 to 6.68). Six months did no better than three. Lung recipients were the exception: three months rather than six raised the risk of infection and high-level DNAaemia, though not significantly of disease. Recipient-seropositive patients had a low rate of cytomegalovirus disease whatever their prophylaxis. The authors emphasise that the reassurance about shorter courses applies to programmes that keep monitoring viral load once prophylaxis stops, and the abstract does not give kidney-specific estimates separately from the pooled non-lung group. For UK kidney units that give six months to mismatched recipients, the study supports a three-month course paired with structured viral surveillance after prophylaxis ends, cutting antiviral exposure without obvious loss of protection.

### 5. [Association of eplet mismatch load and allograft injury in kidney transplant recipients](https://doi.org/10.1093/ckj/sfag341)
[Toth F, Holdaway KJ, Raghavan D, Marineci S, Oygen S, Fornadi K, Molnar MZ. *Clin Kidney J*, 2026. PMID: 42865783.]{.kw-ref}

Most eplet studies count a single outcome. This one combines every early sign of alloimmune injury a modern programme collects: de novo donor-specific antibody, histological rejection, molecular rejection on the Molecular Microscope Diagnostic System, and a raised donor-derived cell-free DNA level. Among 657 adults transplanted at Utah between 2021 and 2024 (30.6% living donor, 84.0% thymoglobulin induction, median calculated panel-reactive antibody 0%), 37.7% met at least one of these criteria within the first year. Eplet load was calculated at HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DQA1 and -DQB1. In adjusted Cox models, every additional mismatched eplet raised the hazard at DRB1 (hazard ratio 1.025, 95% confidence interval 1.011 to 1.038), DQA1 (1.075, 1.025 to 1.127) and DQB1 (1.038, 1.020 to 1.057), and high-load categories carried adjusted hazards of 2.64, 2.24 and 3.13 relative to zero mismatch. Class I associations were weaker and inconsistent: HLA-A was significant only by category and HLA-B and -C only per eplet after adjustment. The full text includes two important checks. Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed weak discrimination at every locus, and in a locus-by-locus comparison eplet load did not outperform conventional antigen-level mismatch at any of the six loci, DRB1 included. The single-centre design, the low-sensitisation population and the composite endpoint all limit how far the results generalise. For UK practice, where allocation still runs on antigen-level matching, this reinforces the biological weight of class II, especially DQ, mismatch, but it does not show that eplet scoring adds predictive information that standard HLA typing does not already provide.

### 6. [Kidney donor profile index (KDPI) score and long-term deceased donor kidney transplant outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trre.2026.101059)
[Raza A, AlDuaij A, Almutairi M, Alruwaili O, Albusaidi AJB, Dwaidari M, Abdulkhaleq T, Sumail RMM, Altoukhi SM, Mohammad S, Alqallaf D, Serhan LF, Mohsin B. *Transplant Rev (Orlando)*, 2026. PMID: 42874429.]{.kw-ref}

The kidney donor profile index is used well beyond the United States as a shorthand for organ quality, so its long-term predictive performance outside its home registry matters. The reviewers searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov from January 2014 to June 2026 for cohorts of at least 100 adult deceased-donor recipients followed for at least three years. They standardised adjusted hazard ratios for death-censored graft failure to a 10-point rise in the index and pooled them with random-effects models using Hartung-Knapp intervals. Thirteen publications qualified, but only five, with 2,902 recipients, supplied estimates that could be combined. Each 10-point increase was associated with a 19% higher hazard of graft failure (hazard ratio 1.19, 95% confidence interval 1.08 to 1.31; I² 43.8%), and the prediction interval of 0.97 to 1.46 means that in some settings the true effect could be close to zero. Restricting the analysis to three studies with explicit long-term follow-up gave a hazard ratio of 1.14 (1.02 to 1.27; I² 14.2%). The comparison of indices above 85% with lower scores was too imprecise to interpret (hazard ratio 2.13, 0.75 to 6.02). Reported C-statistics clustered between 0.54 and 0.62, which shows that the index ranks individual kidneys only modestly better than chance. For UK practice, the conclusion applies to any donor-quality score imported from another system: such scores describe average risk across populations, are poor tools for deciding whether to decline an individual kidney, and need local validation and recalibration.

### 7. [SETI-The Semi-Elective Transplant Initiative: A Systems-Based Approach to Expanding Kidney Transplant Access Through Operational Redesign](https://doi.org/10.1097/SLA.0000000000007235)
[Kaltenmeier C, Hanish SI, Nagaraju S, Barry T, Bolin ED, Cawley PJ, Meenashi Sundaram P, Crawford T, Samy K, Di Sabato D, van der Windt DJ, McGillicuddy JW, Celia A, Baliga PK, Scalea J. *Ann Surg*, 2026. PMID: 42875848.]{.kw-ref}

This paper tackles a familiar constraint: deceased-donor transplantation is reactive, demands urgent mobilisation of hospital resources, and becomes harder to deliver as hospitals run close to capacity, which limits how many organs get used. The Medical University of South Carolina tackled this in two stages. First it expanded machine perfusion (SETI-1). Then it added protected morning theatre access (SETI-2), so that kidneys could be pumped overnight and transplanted as semi-elective cases. The team reviewed 936 adult deceased-donor transplants from January 2022 to June 2025 across the pre-intervention and two intervention eras, using a contemporaneous registry cohort of 12,302 transplants as a reference. Overnight perfusion more than tripled and operative start times moved to between 8 and 10 a.m. Mean cold ischaemia rose from 20.2 to 21.9 hours (p = 0.0039), and donation-after-circulatory-death kidneys with more than 30 hours of cold ischaemia went from 0.5% to 7.7% of transplants. Median kidney donor profile index rose from 29 to 33 to 43 across the eras, showing that the programme was accepting more marginal organs. Delayed graft function (41.4% to 38.2%) and graft failure (5.4% to 3.2%) did not change significantly. In multivariable analysis, donor hypertension predicted graft failure, but cold ischaemia time, circulatory-death donation and era did not. The authors are careful to say that the before-and-after design cannot support causal claims, that the outcome comparisons were underpowered and do not prove equivalence, and that a rise in net organ utilisation was not demonstrated. For UK units facing night-time theatre pressure and high discard rates for marginal kidneys, the model is directly relevant: perfusion used as a scheduling tool, not only as a means of reconditioning organs, could take some of the time pressure out of accepting difficult offers.

### 8. [Associations between OPOs' Responses to Scrutiny about Out of Sequence Allocation and Changes in Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.10.003)
[Stewart DE, Po-Yu Chiang T, Zeiser LB, Lonze BE, Ali N, Berger J, McBride J, Levan ML, Gentry SE, Marklin GF, Hasz RD, Massie AB, Segev DL, Husain SA. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42863631.]{.kw-ref}

Out-of-sequence allocation, in which a procurement organisation steers a kidney it judges at risk of non-use to a chosen centre instead of working down the match list, came under intense scrutiny in the United States in 2025. A high-profile press article appeared in late February, and in early August an OPTN message described the practice as inconsistent with policy. This analysis compared OPTN data from January 2024 to the date of the article with data from the period after the regulatory message, up to February 2026, grouping procurement organisations by how sharply they had cut out-of-sequence allocation. Kidney transplant volume fell 7% in the 33 organisations with large reductions and rose 1% in the other 22 (p = 0.0007 for the difference in changes). Recovery of kidneys from donation-after-circulatory-death donors rose only 1% in the large-reduction group against 14% elsewhere (p < 0.0001 for interaction). The probability that an offered or recovered kidney was transplanted did not change differently between the groups, and non-use among recovered kidneys did not increase. The authors therefore conclude that any loss of transplant volume came from fewer kidneys being recovered in the first place, not from greater difficulty placing the kidneys that were recovered. The study is observational and ecological, so it describes an association with the policy response, not an effect. Its lesson for UK allocation policy on hard-to-place kidneys is that tightening the rules on discretionary offers may reduce donor recoveries, so the effect of any rule change should be measured at the procurement stage as well as in transplants performed.
